subject: Behavioral Economics
title: The Framing Effect in Advertising
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on The Framing Effect in Advertising.

hook.text: Ground beef labeled 75% lean outsells the same beef labeled 25% fat. Same meat, different frame, different sales.

buildup.text: Framing shifts attention. Lean highlights the positive; fat highlights the negative. The frame decides the feeling.

discovery.text: Tversky and Kahneman showed that framing changes risk preferences. A 90% survival rate sounds better than a 10% death.

twist.text: Ethical marketers can frame honestly. Choosing which true fact to lead with is framing. All communication is framed.

climax.text: When any claim sounds great, reframe it in the opposite direction. If it still sounds great, the product is genuine.

punchline.text: The fact didn't change. The frame did.

quiz.question: Why does 75% lean outsell 25% fat beef?
options: Lean beef is actually higher quality
The positive frame shifts attention toward the desirable attribute

details.summary: The framing effect in advertising shows that how a message is presented matters as much as what it says. Describing meat as 95 percent lean versus 5 percent fat changes consumer perception dramatically, even though the information is identical.
details.whyItMatters: Framing is the most fundamental behavioral tool in advertising. By choosing which attributes to emphasize and how to present information, advertisers shape perception without changing the underlying product at all.
takeaways: Identical information presented differently changes consumer preferences
Positive framing increases perceived quality; negative framing triggers avoidance
Effective advertising selects frames that highlight product strengths

faq.question: What is the best frame for advertising a product?
faq.answer: Frame positive attributes in absolute terms and negative attributes in relative terms. Say 95 percent lean not 5 percent fat. Highlight gains for hedonic products and loss prevention for utilitarian products. Match the frame to the audience's motivation.

faq.question: Can consumers learn to see through framing effects?
faq.answer: Partially. Training in reframing helps people recognize when equivalent information is presented differently. But framing effects persist even among educated, aware consumers because they operate quickly at the intuitive level.
